The Realms of the Nine

The Realms of the Nine

“The marks are not merely brands upon flesh — they are maps of dominion. Each city that falls, each breath corrupted, extends the reach of the Nine.”
— Scholar Edrion Vales, Atlas of the Fallen Age

Over the past decades, the Demon Lords have carved their realms across the lands of mortals. Cities, kingdoms, and hidden dominions now bear the Marks of their infernal masters.

Agravorn in Equilara

Once the beating heart of the empire of the gods, Equilara now serves as the seat of the Throne itself and of Agravorn, the self-proclaimed King of Demons.

Agravorn is the mightiest of the Demon Lords, holding the others in check through sheer force and ancient right.

The Throne is seldom spoken of directly, a power beyond even the Nine, hovering above them all like a dark sun.

Kasbeel in Astralan (Velenor)

Kasbeel, the Plaguebringer, rules from the once-radiant city of Astralan, now shrouded in sickly mists.

Poisonous vapors drift through its streets, causing feverish hallucinations that twist beauty into decay. Merchants still flock there, believing Astralan to be a free city, unaware that the haze itself compels them to stay.

The city has become a living organism, pulsing to feed its master’s hunger.

Athera — The War of Two Lords

Dagon in Silverspring

Silverspring lies half-drowned beneath the waters of a vast, unnatural reservoir.

Here reigns Dagon, the Abyssal King, whose colossal serpentine body coils through the depths. Those marked by Dagon mutate slowly: gills open along their throats, scales spread across their flesh, and their eyes begin to glimmer in the dark waters.

They live in precarious stilt-villages above the flooded ruins, whispering prayers to their silent god.

Azzael in Emberstone

To the south rises Emberstone, claimed by Azzael, the Burning Judge.

Since his arrival, the volcano at the city’s heart has never ceased to erupt. Monthly blood rites feed his endless hunger for purification, and his fanatics wage holy war upon Silverspring.

Azzael’s zeal burns brighter than reason. Where he rules, only ash and screams remain.

Caim in the Northern Deep Kingdoms

Far beneath the frozen mountains of the north lie the remnants of the ancient dwarven kingdoms: halls, mines, forge-cities, and deep roads older than most mortal realms.

Here rules Caim, the Iron Lord.

Dwarven flesh resists ordinary demonic binding, and so Caim found other ways to make them obedient. He controls the deep roads, seals the ancient forge-fires, holds clan against clan, and turns ancestral oaths into chains. Entire bloodlines are made responsible for the obedience of a single dwarf.

Caim rules with an iron hand, not through constant slaughter, but by ensuring that every act of resistance threatens something older and more precious than the rebel’s own life.

The undead dominions claim the frozen plains, fortresses, and mountain passes above. Caim and the Lich-Kings are rivals for the north, yet neither has chosen open war.

For now, the dead leave the Deep Kingdoms untouched, and Caim leaves their black fortresses alone.

Their peace is not trust.

It is the pause between two predators deciding which one can afford to strike first.

Usiel in Illumara (Astravar)

Once the city of healing, meditation, and light, Illumara has fallen to Usiel, the Butcher of Hope.

The sacred hush that once inspired peace now suffocates the soul. Despair clings to every wall; even angels would weep here.

Pilgrims who seek solace find only the echoes of their own hopeless prayers.

Malphas in Aerithar (Zehrion)

Malphas, the Crow-King, does not rule Aerithar from a throne.

Aerithar is no permanent city. It is the great wandering gathering of Zehrion, raised anew each year wherever the winds and the clan leaders call the people together. Thousands arrive with tents, herds, banners, stories, rivalries, and secrets.

Malphas has learned to move with them.

His ravens follow the caravans. His spies travel as merchants, servants, healers, wanderers, and clanless refugees. Shadow-priests listen at fires, copy names, collect grudges, and carry whispers from one tribe to another.

Where Aerithar gathers, so does his network.

Malphas rarely commands openly. Instead, he turns suspicion into accusation, rivalry into betrayal, and private knowledge into weapons. A secret spoken beside one fire may reach another clan before sunrise. A promise made beneath one banner may already be known three valleys away.

No clan knows how deeply his servants have entered their ranks.

And so Aerithar still moves freely across Zehrion.

Malphas simply moves with it.

Flauros in Morrdrak

The dead lands of Morrdrak know no open ruler, yet whispers speak of Flauros, the Corrupter of Truth.

He moves unseen among lich-kings and necromancers, spreading doubt and false memory. Where others conquer with armies, Flauros conquers with questions — and beneath his influence, the living rot faster than the dead.

Few have heard his name spoken aloud, and fewer still remember it correctly.

Beleth in the Realm That Cannot Be Found

Of Beleth, the Hidden Demon, almost nothing is known.

He is considered the weakest of the Nine. No visible kingdom bears his banner. No city openly carries his Mark. No army marches beneath his name, and no reliable map records the location of his throne.

That silence frightens even the servants of the other Demon Lords.

Some believe Beleth is merely hiding from his stronger kin. Others fear that weakness has forced him to become patient. Rumors speak of unseen houses, secret pacts, and alliances formed beyond the recognized demonic order.

If those rumors are true, what Beleth is building in the dark may prove even worse than the empire that currently rules the world.

It is never comforting when nothing is heard from a demon.

It means only that no one has yet discovered what he is doing.

Sammael is the Fallen Lord

Of Sammael, the Lord of Battles, little remains but rumor.

He was struck down years ago in a cataclysmic battle, yet soldiers still dream of his horn and awaken with bloodied hands. It is said that his essence lingers in the marches beyond Zehrion, gathering the restless dead and preparing for his return.

Even slain, war itself cannot die.

Coins, Demon Houses, and Bloodhounds

After the fall of the gods, the old order of the world collapsed. Kingdoms broke apart, cities burned, and the old trade roads were swallowed by demons, hunger, and fear. Gold, silver, and inherited wealth lost their meaning in places where bread, water, and walls decided who lived another day.

But over time, a new order took shape.

The Demon Lords do not rule like mortal kings. They do not need love, loyalty, or worship. They only demand that the world continues to function. People must be born, raised, put to work, kept obedient, and harvested when their souls are ripe.

The demons do not enforce this order in everyday life themselves.

For that, there are the Demon Houses.

::

The Demon Houses

The Demon Houses are powerful families and dynasties that rose to power in the decades after the fall. Some descend from old noble bloodlines. Others were once wealthy farming families, military commanders, city captains, mercenary leaders, collaborating officials, or simple opportunists who understood early enough which side would survive.

Today, they rule in the name of the Demon Lords.

They distribute rations, assign labor, control markets, mint coins, keep records, collect debts, monitor travel, and report anyone who might become dangerous to the order. They are not protectors of the people. They are the human instruments of demonic rule.

No one should expect help from a Demon House. Individual members may doubt, regret, or secretly search for another way, but the house itself is part of the system. Its safety, wealth, and survival depend on delivering people to the powers above them.

For most people, the Demon Houses are the visible face of oppression. The demons are distant terror. The Demon Houses are the hand at the door.

Rations and Daily Life

Most people do not work for coins.

A farmer, seamstress, miner, servant, guard, or scribe is rarely paid a wage in the old sense. Instead, they receive bread, water, shelter, tools, simple clothing, and protection. Those who are useful and obedient receive enough to continue living. Those who are not useful quickly fall out of the order.

Rations are therefore more important than wealth.

A ration represents one day of basic survival: food, water, perhaps salt, fuel, or a place within the walls. For common people, this is worth more than any old gold coin.

Bloodsilver

Coins still exist.

They are not used to make the Demon Houses rich. The Demon Houses take what they want. Their power rests on soldiers, records, walls, rations, and the favor of the Demon Lords.

Coins are mainly used by those who need to move within the order: travelers, merchants, mercenaries, messengers, guards, innkeepers, spies, craftsmen, smugglers, and servants of the Demon Houses.

The coins of the demon realms are minted from Bloodsilver.

Bloodsilver comes from Emberstone, the old city of embers, where Azzael, the Burning Judge, now reigns. No one outside Emberstone knows how the metal is made. Some say it is silver that has passed through Azzael’s fire. Others claim it is smelted from the ashes of the condemned. No one knows the truth.

Only one thing is certain: Bloodsilver cannot be forged by ordinary means.

A true coin carries thin red veins within the metal. When held against sunlight, candlelight, or open flame, these veins shimmer like blood beneath the surface. Some coins seem to hold a weak flame inside them.

The stamp of a coin usually shows the symbol of the Demon Lord whose territory recognizes it. But the stamp alone does not make the coin real.

The Bloodsilver does.

To test a coin, one holds it to the light. If the red veins do not glow, the coin is false.

The Value of Coins

Bloodsilver is rare, but it is not treasure in the old sense. A coin matters not because the metal is beautiful, but because it is recognized within the demonic order.

With Bloodsilver, one can buy things outside normal rationing: a better bed, a warm meal, medicine, weapons, information, silence, passage, transport, or a place in a caravan.

On markets, simple goods are often exchanged through labor, barter, or rations. Coins are used mainly when strangers trade with one another, or when someone must be paid who does not belong to the same household, work crew, or duty chain.

A worker lives on rations. An innkeeper accepts Bloodsilver. A mercenary demands Bloodsilver. A scribe may forget a name for Bloodsilver. A gatekeeper may open a side door for Bloodsilver.

But Bloodsilver does not buy freedom.

It buys time, access, and silence.

Markets and Taverns

Markets and taverns are not free places. They exist under the eyes of the Demon Houses.

A tavern is more than an inn. It is a sleeping hall, rumor market, work exchange, checkpoint, and often a place of surveillance. The innkeeper usually holds a license from the ruling house. They may receive travelers, inspect coins, sell rumors, and pass names to the authorities.

When someone pays in a tavern, they are not merely paying for beer and a bed.

They are paying to be tolerated for one night.

Markets are no different. Every trade takes place under the shadow of the house. Anyone caught with false coins, stolen goods, or forbidden wares is not treated as a simple thief.

They have challenged the order.

And those who challenge the order die.

Bloodhounds

To enforce their rule, the Demon Houses rely on more than guards, scribes, and soldiers. Many maintain special hunters and executioners in their service.

Officially, they may be called Trackers, House Hunters, or Enforcers.

The people call them Bloodhounds or Chainhounds.

Bloodhounds are humans, or former humans, changed by demonic marks, blood rites, long exposure to their masters, or willing corruption. They are not full demons, but they are no longer fully human.

They hunt traitors, counterfeiters, escaped debt-workers, rebels, god-believers, Unbound, and anyone who vanishes from the records of the Demon Houses.

Many Bloodhounds can scent blood, fear, guilt, or demonic marks. Some can recognize Bloodsilver by smell alone.

They are proof that the Demon Houses do not rule by violence alone.

They rule by proximity to demons.

The Order of the Demon Realms

The demon realms are not held together by justice. They are held together by hunger, fear, records, and violence.

The Demon Lords stand above all. The Demon Houses keep cities and lands obedient. Rations keep the people alive. Bloodsilver moves travelers, secrets, and favors. Bloodhounds retrieve those who escape the order. And the Marked show everyone what happens to those who resist.

In Destroyed Faith, money is not a sign of freedom.

It is only another tool in a world that has learned to manage people until they are ripe for the harvest.

A World Without Hope

Godless temples and ruins from ages past stand as silent witnesses to the great loss, and the ancient prophecies that once foretold the end have long been forgotten. The memory of the old pantheon lives only in the dreams of the few who still dare to believe in the divine. Paladins and priests have vanished, and only rarely does one find a survivor who still understands divine magic. Still, there are rumors of an ancient prophecy that speaks of the gods’ return—a time when the forgotten light will be reborn. But most people no longer believe. The demons have a firm grip on the world, and the darkness seems insurmountable.
